gaps.question: Section 3 evaluates the predicates by lazy determinization of the transducer, following Snæbjarnarson et al. (2026), without further detail. How do you compute the live, member and cylinder tests in practice? We computed them directly from the codon map: an output is a member when it starts with the target, and every member is also a cylinder because the codon output only grows. Is that right?
gaps.assumption: Do not build a transducer: call setup.transducer.is_live / is_member / is_cylinder (problem/setup.py, CodonTransducer). There is_cylinder == is_member because the codon output only grows, so in this setup no remainder entries ever arise (member implies cylinder) and R stays empty.

gaps.question: Neither prune_M nor prune_tau says how equal weights are ordered by sort_descending, nor whether prune_tau compares W_i >= (1-tau)W_N with exact or tolerant floating-point comparison. How is this done? We assumed: Use a stable descending sort by weight (ties keep insertion order, e.g. numpy argsort(-w, kind='stable')) and an exact >= comparison on cumulative sums computed in that order. In the worst case all covering particles have equal weight, so any tie rule gives the same total min(M, 3^T) * 4^(-3T) (Eq. 49 with equality); tie order only changes which strings are kept. Is that right?
gaps.assumption: Use a stable descending sort by weight (ties keep insertion order, e.g. numpy argsort(-w, kind='stable')) and an exact >= comparison on cumulative sums computed in that order. In the worst case all covering particles have equal weight, so any tie rule gives the same total min(M, 3^T) * 4^(-3T) (Eq. 49 with equality); tie order only changes which strings are kept.

gaps.question: The paper does not say how to handle floating-point error in pps/systematic: sum(pi) may differ from M by rounding, and pi_i may land just below 1 for a particle that should be pinned. How is this done? We assumed: Compute pi in float64; after pps, clip pi to [0,1]; in systematic use u + k for k = 0..M-1 against the cumulative sums and take exactly M (or m) indices via searchsorted on C (side='right'), rescaling C so that C_N = M exactly. Return exactly M distinct survivors whenever |I+| > M. Is that right?
gaps.assumption: Compute pi in float64; after pps, clip pi to [0,1]; in systematic use u + k for k = 0..M-1 against the cumulative sums and take exactly M (or m) indices via searchsorted on C (side='right'), rescaling C so that C_N = M exactly. Return exactly M distinct survivors whenever |I+| > M.

gaps.question: Fig. 10 stops a particle only when it samples EOS, with no cylinder check. Is that intended, so that smc_simple walks every particle to the end of its string? We followed Fig. 10 as written, with sources that stop with probability one (the App. E source stops after exactly 3T symbols). Is that right?
gaps.assumption: Follow Fig. 10 as written: no cylinder shortcut. Particles stop only by sampling EOS. Both sources in setup.py stop with probability one (bigram: 0.02 after each base; worst case: exactly at length 300, as in App. E), so smc_simple halts without it. Adding the shortcut would turn smc_simple into smc_rb. (Updated by the controller after the yardstick review: setup.UNIFORM now stops at 300.)

How is this done? We assumed: Run beam_summing (prune_M and prune_tau) without the decorator so it stays deterministic, matching Fig. 1 and the 'beam search' framing. In this setup it never matters: each target-prefix call extends a particle at most 3 source symbols before it becomes a cylinder, so weights never fall below e^-30 w0. Is that right?
gaps.assumption: Run beam_summing (prune_M and prune_tau) without the decorator so it stays deterministic, matching Fig. 1 and the 'beam search' framing. In this setup it never matters: each target-prefix call extends a particle at most 3 source symbols before it becomes a cylinder, so weights never fall below e^-30 w0.

gaps.question: Table 1 gives the particle-count column: beam_summing (no prune) unbounded; + prune_M fixed M; + prune_tau mass-set (no M); smc_simple and smc_rb fixed M (M initial particles of weight 1/M); beam_swor fixed M (cap per prune); beam_swor_adaptive adaptive m <= M ('nominal' M). For smc_simple/smc_rb, M is the initial particle count (pool size is never increased; resampling keeps the current size). For beam_swor M caps survivors per prune; for beam_swor_adaptive it is the maximum in Eq. 16. Is that right?

gaps.question: Results are averaged over S seeds (8 for Table 2, 64 for Fig. 9(a)), but the paper does not say how seeds map to runs, or whether runs for different M or targets share random numbers. How did you seed the runs? We used one independent random stream per target, per M and per seed. Is that right?
gaps.assumption: One independent run per (target i, M index j, seed k) drawing all randomness from setup.rng(i, j, k) (numpy default_rng([seed, i, j])). Deterministic methods (beam_summing) fill every seed slot with the same value. For systematic sampling draw the permutation and u from that generator; for Bernoulli/categorical draws likewise.

gaps.question: The paper does not say what an implementation should do when every particle dies (a prune or roulette empties the pool before any quotient mass is collected, or a later target-prefix call starts from an empty quotient). Figs. 7-8 only say a failed GPT-2 run contributes Z_hat_s = 0 to the seed average. What happens here? We assumed: Follow the pseudocode literally: an empty Q' gives an empty starting pool, the while loop does not run, A = 0 (plus any re-checked remainder mass), and the recursion continues to |y|. A final Z_hat of 0 is reported as log_z = -inf (never NaN); the seed average then includes a zero, as in Figs. 7-8. Particles with nu(x) = 0 or lambda(x) = 0 are dropped (Fig. 12 line 129). Is that right?
gaps.assumption: Follow the pseudocode literally: an empty Q' gives an empty starting pool, the while loop does not run, A = 0 (plus any re-checked remainder mass), and the recursion continues to |y|. A final Z_hat of 0 is reported as log_z = -inf (never NaN); the seed average then includes a zero, as in Figs. 7-8. Particles with nu(x) = 0 or lambda(x) = 0 are dropped (Fig. 12 line 129).

gaps.question: The DNA bigram source behind f_dna2aa is trained on 'the DNA training corpus', which is not named, and its probabilities (including the stop probability) are not given. Which corpus trained the bigram, and could you share its fitted probabilities? We used a hand-set stand-in over ACGT with stop probability 0.02 after each base, so we can test the paper's claims but not its Table 2 numbers. Is that a reasonable stand-in?
gaps.assumption: Use setup.BIGRAM, a hand-set high-entropy, A/T-rich, CpG-depleted bigram over ACGT with start row (.30,.20,.20,.30, no stop) and stop probability 0.02 after every base (high enough that smc_simple, which walks each particle to EOS, fits the time budget). It is a stand-in, so Table 2's DNA numbers are not reproducible; we test the claims (unbiased, error falls with M, beam_summing is a lower bound). p_dna (GPT-2 on DNA) is not covered.
gaps.blocks: Grading against Table 2's numbers: a hand-set DNA bigram stands in for the unnamed corpus, so today only the paper's claims are checked.

gaps.question: f_dna2aa maps DNA strings to amino-acid strings, but the paper does not give the codon table, the reading frame, how stop codons are handled, or what a trailing partial codon emits. How is f_dna2aa defined? We assumed the standard genetic code in frame 0, read left to right, with stop codons emitting a stop symbol without ending the output, and a trailing partial codon emitting nothing. Is that right?
gaps.assumption: setup.CodonTransducer: standard genetic code, frame 0, codons read left to right; each complete codon emits one amino acid; the three stop codons (TAA, TAG, TGA) emit '*' and do not terminate the output; a trailing partial codon emits nothing. is_member(x,y) = output(x) starts with y; is_cylinder = is_member; is_live also accepts a partial final codon that some codon for the next target symbol extends.

gaps.question: App. E's source puts all its mass on strings of length exactly 3T, but the paper does not write its stop rule as a next-symbol model. How should the source stop? We assumed each base has probability 1/4 and the source stops with probability one at length 3T, never before. Is that right?
gaps.assumption: setup.UNIFORM gives 1/4 per base and stops after exactly 300 bases (p(EOS|x) = 1 at length 300, 0 before), matching App. E's p_X(x) = (1/4)^{3T} over strings of length 3T. The worst case also turns the tail roulette off (kappa = 0): the decomposition is finite, so every method halts, and the paper's exactness argument ignores the roulette. setup.py adds a second worst-case target (WORST_MIX) made of amino acids whose codons share their first two bases, where the same argument holds.
